intro: On Nov 8, 2026, this page was rewritten for readers new to the subject, after usability feedback: it now says what the law means for students, families and staff, and what each side says it protects. An AI agent wrote it from saved copies of its sources. Separate AI checkers, which never saw the drafting, then checked it in rounds. In this trial, no person checked the facts. Here is what the checkers did, what they found, and what is still open.

sections.title: What we checked
paras: Each round runs the same checks. A page passes a round only when every check passes. After that, we fix only sentences that misstate a source or break our writing rules, and fresh checkers look again at just those sentences: one for facts, and one that asks of each changed summary line whether we would write it the same way about the other side. Other suggestions wait for the next full round.
head: Check
What it does
Pass mark
rows: Code confirms that every sentence cites a source passage or is labeled as our analysis, that quotes match word for word, that saved files match their fingerprints, and that the reading level is about grade 8 or lower.
A separate AI checker sees only this page and the source passages. For each sentence it must copy the exact words that support it, and code confirms those words are really there.

Three more AI checkers. One speaks up for the law's supporters, one for its critics, and a neutral editor checks the rules. The editor also asks of each sentence: would we write it the same way about the other side?
Both side reviewers give at least 4 of 5, and no serious problem

Each round, we hid errors in a copy of the page, such as a wrong deadline, an exception the law doesn't make, a misquoted survey answer and a sentence recommending an option. The fact-checker had to find them without knowing they were there.

sections.title: What each round found
paras: No fact-check found a claim that its sources didn't support, only sentences that said more than the sources did. Rounds 1 to 4 checked earlier versions. Round 5 checked the rewrite for new readers, and round 6 checked one evidence label that all three panelists asked us to change.

sections.title: What's still open
paras: These suggestions change a card, a label or the balance between sides, so they wait for the next full round. Some contradict each other; we list both views rather than pick one quietly.
items: Reviewers disagree on two evidence labels: supporters want card 2's and card 5's labels worded differently; critics accept them. Labels change only in a full round.
Card 2's title says "friendships"; the survey's words are "in-person social interactions". Titles change only in a full round.
The K-8 line notes the law dropped e-readers from its list of examples; the law's general definition may still cover them.
Our sources give no phone number or email for lawmakers or school districts, so the page can't list them.
The State School Superintendent's job isn't described in any source we saved.

sections.title: What this can't do
paras: All the checkers are AI, like the writer, so they may share blind spots. Hiding test errors measures only the kinds of errors we thought to hide.
The checkers compare this page with the sources we saved. They can't tell what is missing from those sources.
The two side reviewers stand in for real people's views. They are not real people.

sections.title: See every report
paras: Every check, report and fix is public in the project's repository, in trials/001-hb1009-high-school-cellphones/verification.md.

stateLine: Every sentence on this page has a current check. A sentence is checked again whenever it or its source changes.
